events.enhanced_description: On May 6, 1960, U.S. President Dwight D. Eisenhower signed the Civil Rights Act of 1960 into law, aimed at improving voting rights and addressing racial discrimination in the United States.
events.name: Civil Rights Act of 1960

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1960, the U.S. nuclear-powered submarine USS Triton, commanded by Captain Edward L. Beach Jr., completed the first underwater circumnavigation of the Earth, a remarkable feat in naval exploration.
events.name: USS Triton circumnavigation

events.enhanced_description: On May 11, 1960, four Mossad agents abducted fugitive Nazi war criminal Adolf Eichmann in Buenos Aires, Argentina, leading to his trial in Israel and conviction for crimes against humanity.
events.name: Abduction of Adolf Eichmann

events.enhanced_description: On May 13, 1960, a joint Swiss and Austrian expedition achieved the first ascent of Dhaulagiri, the world's seventh highest mountain, marking a significant milestone in the history of mountaineering.
events.name: First ascent of Dhaulagiri

events.enhanced_description: On May 14, 1960, the Kenyan African National Congress Party was founded in Nairobi, Kenya, as three political parties joined forces to advocate for independence and democratic governance in the country.
events.name: Founding of Kenyan African National Congress Party

events.enhanced_description: On May 15, 1960, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 4 into orbit, contributing to the space race and advancing the field of space exploration.
events.name: Launch of Sputnik 4

events.enhanced_description: On May 16, 1960, Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev publicly demanded an apology from U.S. President Dwight D. Eisenhower regarding U-2 reconnaissance flights over the Soviet Union. This demand effectively led to the cancellation of their scheduled summit meeting in Paris, escalating tensions during the Cold War.
events.name: Khrushchev demands an apology from Eisenhower

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1960, Real Madrid defeated Eintracht Frankfurt 7-3 at Hampden Park in Glasgow, securing their fifth consecutive European Cup title. This match is remembered as one of the greatest finals in the history of European football.
events.name: Real Madrid wins 1960 European Cup

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1960, the Valdivia earthquake, measuring 9.5 Mw, struck Chile, causing extreme destruction and triggering a massive tsunami. It remains the most powerful earthquake ever recorded, with widespread impacts felt across the Pacific.
events.name: Valdivia earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On May 27, 1960, a bloodless military coup in Turkey led to the removal of President Celâl Bayar and the installation of General Cemal Gürsel as the head of state. This event marked a significant shift in Turkish politics and governance.
events.name: Military coup in Turkey

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1960, General Cemal Gürsel formed the 24th government of Turkey, which was primarily composed of technocrats. This government was established following the military coup that ousted the previous administration.
events.name: Cemal Gürsel forms new government

events.enhanced_description: On June 1, 1960, New Zealand's first television station commenced broadcasting in Auckland. This marked a significant milestone in the country's media landscape, bringing television entertainment and information to the public.
events.name: New Zealand's first television station begins broadcasting

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1960, the Lake Bodom murders occurred in Finland, where three teenagers were brutally killed while camping near the lake. This unsolved case remains one of Finland's most infamous criminal mysteries.
events.name: Lake Bodom murders

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1960, Typhoon Mary struck China, resulting in the deaths of approximately 1,600 people. This devastating storm caused widespread destruction and highlighted the vulnerability of coastal regions to severe weather events.
events.name: Typhoon Mary strikes China

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1960, the Hagerty Incident occurred when a car carrying U.S. officials was mobbed by protesters outside Tokyo's Haneda Airport. The situation escalated, requiring a U.S. Marine helicopter for their rescue amid ongoing protests against the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty.
events.name: Hagerty Incident

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1960, the June 15 Incident took place during massive protests against the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty, where radical student activists attempted to storm the National Diet compound, resulting in a violent clash with police and the tragic death of student Michiko Kanba.
events.name: June 15 Incident

events.enhanced_description: On June 16, 1960, Alfred Hitchcock's landmark thriller film 'Psycho' premiered in the United States. The film is renowned for its innovative narrative structure and psychological depth, significantly influencing the horror genre.
events.name: Premiere of Psycho

events.enhanced_description: On June 19, 1960, the new U.S.-Japan Security Treaty was automatically ratified following its passage in the Lower House of the Diet. This treaty solidified the military alliance between the two nations amidst rising tensions in the region.
events.name: U.S.-Japan Security Treaty ratified

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, 1960, the Mali Federation, comprising the Sudanese Republic (modern-day Mali) and Senegal, gained independence from France. This federation, however, was short-lived as it dissolved shortly after independence.
events.name: Mali Federation gains independence

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, 1960, Floyd Patterson made history by becoming the first boxer to regain the world heavyweight championship, defeating Ingemar Johansson by knockout in New York City. This victory solidified Patterson's legacy in the boxing world.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Floyd Patterson regains heavyweight championship

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1960, the Quebec general election resulted in the defeat of the ruling Union nationale, led by Antonio Barrette, by the Quebec Liberal Party under Jean Lesage. This election marked the beginning of the 'Quiet Revolution' in Quebec, a period of significant social and political change.
events.name: Quebec general election

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1960, Japanese Prime Minister Nobusuke Kishi announced his resignation amidst widespread protests against the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty. His departure marked a significant moment in Japanese politics during a time of national unrest.
events.name: Nobusuke Kishi resigns

events.enhanced_description: On June 30, 1960, Joseph Kasa-Vubu was elected as the first President of the newly independent Democratic Republic of the Congo. His presidency marked a significant transition for the nation following its liberation from Belgian colonial rule.

locations.name: Kinshasa, Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo

events.name: Joseph Kasa-Vubu elected President

events.enhanced_description: On June 26, 1960, Somaliland, formerly known as British Somaliland, received its independence from the United Kingdom. Shortly thereafter, it united with the Trust Territory of Somalia to form the Somali Republic.

image.caption: Page 2 of the Somaliland Order in Council (S.I. No. 1060 of 1960), a legal document.
image.date_qualification: Document dated 1960/06/23; this is not a photograph of the independence ceremony on 26 June 1960.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Somaliland gains independence

events.enhanced_description: On June 26, 1960, the State of Somaliland, formerly the British Somaliland protectorate, gained independence from the United Kingdom. Shortly thereafter, it united with the Trust Territory of Somalia to form the Somali Republic.
events.name: Independence of Somaliland

events.enhanced_description: On June 26, 1960, the Malagasy Republic (Madagascar) achieved independence from France. This marked a significant step in the decolonization movement across Africa during the 20th century.
events.name: Independence of Madagascar

events.enhanced_description: On June 28, 1960, King Bhumibol Adulyadej of Thailand arrived in Washington, D.C. for a four-day royal visit to the United States. This visit was significant in strengthening diplomatic relations between Thailand and the U.S.
events.name: King Bhumibol's visit to the U.S.

events.enhanced_description: On June 30, 1960, the Belgian Congo gained independence from Belgium, becoming the Republic of the Congo (Léopoldville). This transition marked the beginning of a tumultuous period, including a civil war shortly thereafter.

locations.name: Kinshasa, Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo

events.name: Belgian Congo gains independence

events.enhanced_description: On June 30, 1960, the Belgian Congo gained independence from Belgium, becoming the Republic of the Congo (Léopoldville). This transition was marred by immediate civil unrest and conflict, leading to a civil war.

locations.name: Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo

events.name: Independence of the Belgian Congo

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1960, Ghana transitioned from a constitutional monarchy to a republic, with Kwame Nkrumah serving as its first President. This change marked a significant moment in Ghana's post-colonial history.
events.name: Ghana becomes a republic

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1960, the Trust Territory of Somaliland, formerly Italian Somaliland, gained independence from Italy. This event was part of a larger movement towards unification with the recently independent State of Somaliland.
events.name: Independence of the Trust Territory of Somaliland

events.enhanced_description: On July 3, 1960, Australian driver Jack Brabham won the French Grand Prix, driving a Cooper T53. This victory was part of his successful Formula One career and contributed to his reputation as one of the sport's greats.

locations.name: Le Mans, Pays de la Loire, France

events.name: Jack Brabham wins French Grand Prix

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1960, the new 50-star flag of the United States was officially flown over Philadelphia for the first time, following Hawaii's admission as the 50th state in August 1959. This event symbolized the expansion of the United States.
events.name: 50-star flag flown in Philadelphia

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1960, the Soviet Union national football team defeated Yugoslavia 2-1 in Paris to win the inaugural UEFA European Championship. This victory marked a significant achievement in Soviet sports history.
events.name: Soviet Union wins first UEFA European Championship

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1960, during the Congo Crisis, Moïse Tshombe declared the province of Katanga independent, seeking support from Belgium. This declaration intensified the conflict in the newly independent Democratic Republic of the Congo.

locations.name: Lubumbashi, Democratic Republic of the Congo

events.name: Katanga declares independence

events.enhanced_description: On July 12, 1960, Chin Peng, a prominent leader of the Malayan Communist Party, was exiled from Malaysia to Thailand as the Malayan state of emergency was lifted. This marked a significant moment in the history of communist movements in Southeast Asia.
events.name: Chin Peng exiled from Malaysia

events.enhanced_description: On July 14, 1960, the United Nations Security Council decided to send troops to Katanga to oversee the withdrawal of Belgian forces amid the ongoing Congo Crisis. This intervention was part of the UN's efforts to stabilize the region.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: UN Security Council sends troops to Katanga

events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1960, Ceylon elected Sirimavo Bandaranaike as Prime Minister, making her the world's first female head of government. Her election was a landmark moment in the history of women's political representation.
events.name: Sirimavo Bandaranaike elected Prime Minister

events.enhanced_description: On July 21, 1960, English navigator Francis Chichester won the first Single-Handed Trans-Atlantic Race, arriving in New York aboard Gypsy Moth III after a record solo crossing of 40 days. This achievement showcased the spirit of adventure and exploration.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Francis Chichester wins Single-Handed Trans-Atlantic Race

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1960, the Woolworth Company's lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, served its first black customer, marking a significant moment in the Civil Rights Movement. This event followed a series of sit-ins that challenged segregation.
events.name: Woolworth's lunch counter serves first black customer

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1960, the 1960 Republican National Convention in Chicago nominated Vice President Richard Nixon as its candidate for President of the United States, with Henry Cabot Lodge Jr. as his running mate. This convention set the stage for the upcoming presidential election.

image.caption: Back of an entrance ticket for the 1960 Republican National Convention in Chicago.
image.date_qualification: Dated 1960; the record gives a year, not a specific day.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: 1960 Republican National Convention

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1960, Dahomey (now Benin) gained independence from France. This event was part of the wave of decolonization that swept across Africa during the mid-20th century.
events.name: Independence of Dahomey

events.enhanced_description: On August 3, 1960, Niger achieved independence from France. This marked a significant step in the country's journey towards self-governance and sovereignty.
events.name: Independence of Niger

events.enhanced_description: On August 5, 1960, Upper Volta (now Burkina Faso) gained independence from France. This event was part of the broader decolonization movement across Africa during the 20th century.
events.name: Independence of Upper Volta

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1960, Albert Kalonji declared the independence of the Autonomous State of South Kasai from the newly independent Democratic Republic of the Congo, amidst a backdrop of ethnic tensions and political instability.

locations.name: Léopoldville, Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo

events.name: Albert Kalonji declares the independence of the Autonomous State of South Kasai

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1960, the Ivory Coast officially gained independence from France, marking a significant step in the decolonization of West Africa and the establishment of a sovereign state.
events.name: The Ivory Coast becomes independent from France

events.enhanced_description: On August 9, 1960, a coup d'état in Laos led to the overthrow of the government, exacerbating the political turmoil in the region during the Cold War and leading to increased foreign intervention.
events.name: The government of Laos is overthrown in a coup

events.enhanced_description: On August 11, 1960, Chad achieved independence from France, joining a wave of African nations gaining sovereignty and marking a new chapter in its national history.
events.name: Chad becomes independent from France

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1960, Ubangi-Shari declared its independence from France, officially becoming the Central African Republic, a significant event in the decolonization of Africa.
events.name: Ubangi-Shari becomes independent from France, as the Central African Republic

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1960, Middle Congo gained independence from France, becoming the Republic of Congo, a pivotal moment in the wave of independence movements sweeping across Africa.
events.name: Middle Congo becomes independent from France, as the Republic of Congo (Congo-Brazzaville)

events.enhanced_description: On August 16, 1960, Cyprus gained independence from British rule, marking a significant moment in the island's history and its complex geopolitical landscape.
events.name: Cyprus receives its independence from the United Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: On August 17, 1960, The Beatles commenced a 48-night residency at the Indra Club in Hamburg, West Germany, which played a crucial role in their early development and exposure to a wider audience.
events.name: The Beatles begin a residency at the Indra Club in Hamburg

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1960, Senegal declared its independence from the Mali Federation, asserting its sovereignty and marking a significant moment in the history of West African nations.
events.name: Senegal breaks away from the Mali Federation

events.enhanced_description: The 1960 Summer Olympic Games, held in Rome, Italy, commenced on August 25, 1960, marking the first Olympics held in a city that had previously hosted the Games in 1900.
events.name: The 1960 Summer Olympic Games begin in Rome

events.enhanced_description: On August 29, 1960, Hurricane Donna struck Florida and New England, resulting in the deaths of 50 people and causing extensive damage, highlighting the destructive power of hurricanes in the region.
events.name: Hurricane Donna kills 50 people in Florida and New England

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1960, two American citizens, Martin and Mitchell, defected to the Soviet Union, highlighting the tensions of the Cold War and the allure of communism for some disillusioned individuals. Their defection sparked debates about loyalty and ideology during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Martin and Mitchell defection

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1960, U.S. President Dwight D. Eisenhower formally dedicated the Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, which had been activated by NASA earlier that year. This center would play a pivotal role in the United States' space exploration efforts, including the Apollo program.
events.name: Dedication of the Marshall Space Flight Center

events.enhanced_description: On September 9, 1960, the first regular season game of the American Football League took place at Nickerson Field in Boston, Massachusetts. The Denver Broncos triumphed over the Boston Patriots with a score of 13-10, marking the beginning of a new chapter in professional football.
events.name: First American Football League Game

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1960, during the Rome Summer Olympics, Ethiopian runner Abebe Bikila made history by winning the gold medal in the marathon while running barefoot. His victory marked him as the first athlete from Sub-Saharan Africa to win an Olympic gold medal, inspiring generations to come.
events.name: Abebe Bikila Wins Olympic Marathon

events.enhanced_description: On September 14, 1960, Colonel Joseph Mobutu seized power in the Republic of the Congo through a military coup. This event marked the beginning of Mobutu's long and controversial rule, which would significantly impact the political landscape of the nation.
events.name: Joseph Mobutu's Military Coup

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1960, the first international Summer Paralympics, known as the 9th International Stoke Mandeville Games, opened in Rome, Italy. This event marked a significant milestone in the recognition and inclusion of athletes with disabilities in competitive sports.
events.name: First International Summer Paralympics

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1960, Mexican President Adolfo López Mateos announced the nationalization of the country's electricity supply system. This move aimed to improve the efficiency and accessibility of electricity across Mexico, reflecting a broader trend of nationalization in Latin America during this period.
events.name: Nationalization of Electricity in Mexico

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1960, Mali, the last remaining member of the Mali Federation after Senegal's withdrawal, declared its full independence as the Republic of Mali. This event marked a significant step in the decolonization process in Africa.
events.name: Mali Declares Independence

events.enhanced_description: On September 26, 1960, the first live televised presidential debate took place between John F. Kennedy and Richard Nixon in Chicago, Illinois. This landmark event transformed the way political campaigns were conducted in the United States, highlighting the importance of media presence.
events.name: First Televised Presidential Debate

events.enhanced_description: On September 29, 1960, during a session of the United Nations General Assembly, Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev famously banged his shoe on a desk in protest. This dramatic outburst occurred while British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan was speaking, symbolizing the heightened tensions of the Cold War.
events.name: Khrushchev's Shoe-Banging Incident

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1960, Nigeria achieved independence from the United Kingdom, with Nnamdi Azikiwe becoming its first native-born Governor-General. This event marked a significant milestone in Nigeria's history and the broader decolonization movement across Africa.
events.name: Nigeria Gains Independence

events.enhanced_description: On October 3, 1960, Jânio Quadros was elected President of Brazil for a five-year term. His presidency would be marked by controversial policies and a sudden resignation that would lead to significant political upheaval in Brazil.
events.name: Jânio Quadros Elected President of Brazil

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1960, Nigeria became the 99th member of the United Nations. This membership symbolized Nigeria's commitment to participating in global governance and international cooperation following its independence.
events.name: Nigeria Joins the United Nations

events.enhanced_description: On October 14, 1960, presidential candidate John F. Kennedy first suggested the idea for the Peace Corps, a program aimed at promoting world peace and friendship through volunteer service. This initiative would later become a hallmark of his presidency.
events.name: John F. Kennedy Proposes Peace Corps

events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1960, a catastrophic explosion occurred at the Baikonur Cosmodrome, killing at least 92 people involved in the Soviet space program. This tragic event, known as the Nedelin catastrophe, highlighted the dangers of early space exploration efforts.
events.name: Nedelin Catastrophe

events.enhanced_description: In late October 1960, Very Severe Cyclonic Storm Ten made landfall in East Pakistan, causing widespread devastation just weeks after a previous storm had already impacted the region. The storm surge exacerbated the humanitarian crisis in the area.
events.name: Very Severe Cyclonic Storm Ten

events.enhanced_description: In the 1960 United States presidential election, Democratic Senator John F. Kennedy narrowly defeated Republican Vice President Richard Nixon. This election was notable for its significant media coverage, including the first-ever televised presidential debates.

image.caption: Map of the Electoral College results of the 1960 U.S. presidential election.
image.date_qualification: 14 September 2008 is identified as the upload date, not the date of the election or a depicted event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: 1960 United States presidential election

events.enhanced_description: On November 14, 1960, Belgium threatened to withdraw from the United Nations in response to criticism regarding its colonial policies in the Republic of the Congo. This incident highlighted the tensions surrounding decolonization in Africa during this period.
events.name: Belgium threatens to leave the United Nations

events.enhanced_description: On November 22, 1960, the United Nations expressed its support for the government of Joseph Kasavubu and Joseph Mobutu in the Democratic Republic of the Congo amid rising political instability. This support was crucial during a time of significant turmoil following the country's independence.

locations.name: Kinshasa, Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo

events.name: United Nations supports the government of Joseph Kasavubu and Joseph Mobutu

events.enhanced_description: In the 1960 New Zealand general election held on November 26, the National Party, led by Keith Holyoake, defeated the incumbent Labour Party after just three years in power. This election marked a significant shift in New Zealand's political landscape.
events.name: 1960 New Zealand general election

events.enhanced_description: On November 28, 1960, Mauritania officially gained independence from France, marking a significant milestone in the decolonization of Africa. This event was part of a larger wave of independence movements across the continent during the 1960s.
events.name: Mauritania becomes independent of France

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1960, Patrice Lumumba, the deposed premier of the Republic of the Congo, was arrested by troops loyal to Colonel Joseph Mobutu. This event marked a critical moment in the political turmoil that engulfed the country following its independence.

locations.name: Kinshasa, Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo

events.name: Patrice Lumumba arrested

events.enhanced_description: On December 2, 1960, U.S. President Dwight D. Eisenhower authorized the allocation of $1 million for the relief and resettlement of Cuban refugees arriving in Florida. This decision was part of the U.S. response to the Cuban Revolution.
events.name: U.S. President Eisenhower authorizes aid for Cuban refugees

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1960, the Soviet Union vetoed Mauritania's admission to the United Nations, reflecting the geopolitical tensions of the Cold War and the complexities surrounding newly independent nations seeking international recognition.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Soviet Union vetoes Mauritania's admission to the UN

events.enhanced_description: On December 7, 1960, the United Nations Security Council convened at the request of the Soviet Union to discuss demands for the immediate release of former Congolese Premier Patrice Lumumba. This session underscored the international concern over Lumumba's fate amidst the Congo crisis.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: UN Security Council session on Lumumba's release

events.enhanced_description: On December 8, 1960, Mary Martin's production of Peter Pan was aired as a stand-alone 2-hour special on NBC, marking a departure from its previous presentation as part of an anthology series. This televised version allowed for repeated broadcasts and showcased the talents of the original Broadway cast.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Mary Martin's Peter Pan presented on NBC

events.enhanced_description: On December 9, 1960, riots erupted in Algeria during French President Charles de Gaulle's visit, resulting in 127 deaths. The unrest reflected the deep divisions and tensions in Algeria as it struggled for independence from French colonial rule.
events.name: Riots during Charles de Gaulle's visit to Algeria

events.enhanced_description: On December 13, 1960, while Emperor Haile Selassie was visiting Brazil, a coup attempt was led by his Imperial Bodyguard, the Kebur Zabagna, who proclaimed his son, Crown Prince Asfaw Wossen Taffari, as the new emperor. This event highlighted the internal strife within Ethiopia's monarchy.

image.caption: Portrait of Brigadier-General Mengistu Neway, commander of the Imperial Guard and a leader of the 1960 Ethiopian coup attempt.
image.date_qualification: before 1961 (as recorded; not a specific year or date)
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: 1960 Ethiopian coup attempt

events.enhanced_description: On December 14, 1960, Antoine Gizenga declared himself the premier of the Democratic Republic of the Congo amidst the ongoing political turmoil following independence. His proclamation was part of the broader struggle for power in the newly independent nation.

locations.name: Kinshasa, Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo

events.name: Antoine Gizenga proclaims himself premier

events.enhanced_description: On December 15, 1960, King Mahendra of Nepal dismissed the democratic government and assumed direct control of the country. This move marked a significant shift in Nepal's political landscape, leading to a period of autocratic rule.
events.name: King Mahendra of Nepal deposes democratic government

events.enhanced_description: On December 16, 1960, U.S. Secretary of State Christian Herter announced that the United States would commit five nuclear submarines and eighty Polaris missiles to NATO defense by the end of 1963. This announcement underscored the U.S. commitment to collective security during the Cold War.
events.name: U.S. Secretary of State announces military commitments

events.enhanced_description: On December 17, 1960, troops loyal to Emperor Haile Selassie successfully quelled the coup attempt that had begun on December 13. Upon his return from Brazil, the Emperor reinstated his authority and absolved his son of any wrongdoing.
events.name: Troops loyal to Haile Selassie overcome coup

events.enhanced_description: On December 19, 1960, a devastating fire broke out on the USS Constellation, the U.S. Navy's largest aircraft carrier, while it was under construction at the Brooklyn Navy Yard. The incident resulted in the deaths of 50 workers and injuries to 150 others.
events.name: Fire at the USS Constellation

events.enhanced_description: On December 23, 1960, Hilkka Saarinen was murdered in Krootila, Finland, in a case that became known as the 'oven homicide.' The case drew significant media attention and highlighted issues of crime and justice in Finland.
events.name: Hilkka Saarinen murder case

events.enhanced_description: In January 1961, the Soviet Union implemented a significant monetary reform aimed at stabilizing its economy. This reform was part of broader efforts to address economic challenges and improve the efficiency of the planned economy.
events.name: Monetary Reform in the Soviet Union

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1961, President Dwight D. Eisenhower announced the severance of diplomatic and consular relations with Cuba, marking a significant escalation in tensions between the two nations. This decision laid the groundwork for the subsequent U.S. embargo and the Cold War standoff.
events.name: U.S. Severing Relations with Cuba

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1961, Aero Flight 311, a Douglas DC-3C, crashed near Kvevlax, Finland, while approaching Vaasa Airport, resulting in the deaths of all 25 individuals on board. The investigation revealed pilot error due to exhaustion and alcohol consumption, marking it as Finland's deadliest air disaster.
events.name: Aero Flight 311 Crash

events.enhanced_description: In 1961, Italian sculptor Alfredo Fioravanti confessed at the U.S. Consulate in Rome to being part of the team that forged the Etruscan terracotta warriors displayed at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. This revelation raised significant questions about the authenticity of the museum's collection.
events.name: Confession of Alfredo Fioravanti

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1961, Patrice Lumumba, the first Prime Minister of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, was assassinated, marking a pivotal moment in the country's tumultuous post-colonial history. His death had profound implications for Congo's political landscape and international relations during the Cold War.
events.name: Assassination of Patrice Lumumba

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1961, a junta composed of two army officers and four civilians took control of the government in El Salvador, ousting a previous junta that had ruled for just three months. This takeover was part of a broader struggle against perceived leftist influences in the country.
events.name: El Salvador Junta Takeover

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1961, Sabena Flight 548 crashed near Brussels, Belgium, resulting in the deaths of 73 individuals, including the entire United States figure skating team. This tragedy highlighted the risks associated with air travel during this period.
events.name: Sabena Flight 548 Crash

events.enhanced_description: In 1961, American soul singer Jackie Wilson was shot and seriously wounded at his Manhattan apartment by his girlfriend, Juanita Jones. This incident shocked the music community and raised concerns about the pressures faced by artists in the public eye.
events.name: Jackie Wilson Shooting Incident

events.enhanced_description: In March and April 1961, drilling for Project Mohole was undertaken off the coast of Guadalupe Island, Mexico. This ambitious scientific project aimed to reach the Mohorovičić discontinuity, providing insights into the Earth's crust and mantle.

image.caption: Model of the Mohole drilling platform.
image.date_qualification: Image date supplied as 1965; this is not a depiction date for the 1961 drilling event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Drilling for Project Mohole

events.enhanced_description: In 1961, the first U.S. Polaris submarines arrived at Holy Loch, Scotland, marking a significant development in the Cold War naval strategy. This deployment underscored the United States' commitment to NATO and its deterrent capabilities in Europe.
events.name: Arrival of U.S. Polaris submarines

events.enhanced_description: In 1961, Monash University in Melbourne, Australia, welcomed its first students, becoming one of the largest universities in the country. The establishment of this institution marked a significant expansion of higher education in Australia.
events.name: Monash University opens

events.enhanced_description: In 1961, the Union of Peoples of Angola, led by Holden Roberto, launched attacks on strategic locations in northern Angola, marking the beginning of the colonial war against Portuguese rule. This conflict would eventually lead to Angola's independence.
events.name: The Union of Peoples of Angola attacks

events.enhanced_description: In 1961, South Africa officially became a republic, severing its ties with the Commonwealth of Nations. This transition marked a significant shift in the country's political landscape during the apartheid era.
events.name: South Africa becomes a republic

events.enhanced_description: In 1961, President John F. Kennedy met with French President Charles de Gaulle in Paris, discussing various international issues including NATO and the Cold War. This meeting was pivotal in shaping Franco-American relations during the early 1960s.
events.name: Kennedy and de Gaulle meet

events.enhanced_description: In 1961, Benfica triumphed over FC Barcelona with a score of 3-2 at Wankdorf Stadium in Bern, winning the 1960-61 European Cup. This victory solidified Benfica's status as a dominant force in European football.
events.name: Benfica wins European Cup

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1961, a train traveling from Paris to Strasbourg derailed near Vitry-le-François, resulting in the tragic deaths of 24 individuals and injuring 109 others. This incident highlighted the safety concerns surrounding railway travel in France during this period.
events.name: A Paris-to-Strasbourg train derails near Vitry-le-François

events.enhanced_description: In 1961, the New Democratic Party (NDP) was established in Winnipeg, Manitoba, through the merger of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (CCF) and the Canadian Labour Congress. This marked a significant shift in Canadian politics, introducing a social democratic alternative to the traditional parties.
events.name: The New Democratic Party of Canada is founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1961, Ireland submitted its first application to join the European Economic Community, marking a significant step in its economic and political integration with Europe. This application reflected Ireland's desire to enhance trade and cooperation with other European nations.
events.name: Ireland applies to join the European Economic Community

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1961, the formerly British Southern Cameroons gained independence from the United Kingdom and united with French Cameroun to form the Federal Republic of Cameroon. This event is celebrated as Unification Day, marking a significant step in the country's history.
events.name: Unification Day in Cameroon

events.enhanced_description: In 1961, baseball player Roger Maris of the New York Yankees hit his 61st home run during the last game of the season against the Boston Red Sox. This achievement set a new record for the longer baseball season, surpassing Babe Ruth's previous record.
events.name: Roger Maris Hits 61st Home Run

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1961, Mongolia and Mauritania were admitted as member states to the United Nations, expanding the organization's global representation and influence. This event marked a significant step in the post-colonial era of international relations.
events.name: Mongolia and Mauritania Join the United Nations

events.enhanced_description: During the Berlin Crisis in 1961, a tense standoff occurred at Checkpoint Charlie between Soviet and American tanks, escalating Cold War tensions. This confrontation highlighted the precarious state of East-West relations in a divided Berlin.

image.caption: U.S. Army tanks face off against Soviet armor at Checkpoint Charlie in Berlin.
image.credit: U.S. Army photo Photo Credit: USAMHI — http://www.army.mil/article/46993/standoff-in-berlin-october-1961/
image.date_qualification: October 1961, as stated in the image description; image_date is empty.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Berlin Crisis: Confrontation at Checkpoint Charlie

events.enhanced_description: Fahrettin Özdilek was appointed as the acting prime minister of Turkey on January 1, 1961. His tenure was marked by efforts to stabilize the government following a period of political upheaval.
events.name: Fahrettin Özdilek Becomes Acting Prime Minister of Turkey

events.enhanced_description: In 1961, Devrim, the first car designed and produced in Turkey, was released. The project was completed in just 130 days, showcasing the country's burgeoning automotive industry and engineering capabilities.
events.name: Release of Devrim, Turkey's First Car

events.enhanced_description: In 1961, the Soviet Union issued a diplomatic note to Finland proposing military cooperation, leading to heightened tensions during the Cold War. This event underscored the strategic importance of Finland in the geopolitical landscape of the era.
events.name: The Note Crisis

events.enhanced_description: In 1961, Joseph Stalin's body was removed from the Lenin Mausoleum in Moscow, symbolizing a significant shift in Soviet politics and public sentiment following his death. This act reflected the de-Stalinization efforts initiated by Nikita Khrushchev.
events.name: Removal of Stalin's Body from Lenin Mausoleum

events.enhanced_description: In 1961, the U.S. Interstate Commerce Commission's federal order banning segregation at all interstate public facilities officially came into effect. This landmark decision was a significant step towards civil rights and equality in the United States.
events.name: U.S. Interstate Commerce Commission Segregation Ban

events.enhanced_description: In 1961, KVN, Russia's longest-running television show, aired for the first time on Soviet television. The show became a cultural phenomenon, combining humor and competition, and has continued to entertain audiences for decades.

image.caption: Alexander Maslyakov, host and producer of KVN.
image.credit: Presidential Press and Information Office of Russia. — http://eng.kremlin.ru/photo/1754?page=9
image.date_qualification: A 2013 portrait at the opening of the Planet KVN Moscow Youth Centre, not a depiction of the show's first broadcast.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: KVN TV Show Aired for the First Time

events.enhanced_description: In 1961, the city of Stalingrad was officially renamed Volgograd, reflecting the political changes in the Soviet Union following the death of Joseph Stalin. This renaming symbolized a shift away from Stalinist policies and a move towards de-Stalinization.
events.name: Stalingrad Renamed Volgograd

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1961, Tanganyika gained independence from the United Kingdom, becoming a Commonwealth realm with Julius Nyerere as its first Prime Minister. This event marked a significant step in the decolonization of Africa.
events.name: Tanganyika gains independence

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1961, the Australian federal election resulted in the re-election of Robert Menzies' Liberal/Country Coalition Government with a narrow one-seat majority over the Labor Party led by Arthur Calwell. This election is noted for its closeness, a rarity in Australian political history.

image.caption: Map showing the winning margin in each electorate in the 1961 Australian federal election.
image.date_qualification: Election-results map, not a contemporary photograph of election activity. Original image date: 2023-05-02.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Australian federal election

events.enhanced_description: In 1961, Adolf Eichmann was pronounced guilty of crimes against humanity by an Israeli war crimes tribunal for his role in orchestrating the Holocaust. This landmark trial highlighted the importance of accountability for war crimes and the ongoing impact of the Holocaust on global consciousness.
events.name: Adolf Eichmann's trial verdict

events.enhanced_description: In early 1961, Indonesian President Sukarno announced his intention to take West Irian by force if necessary, reflecting the tensions surrounding the region's status. This declaration set the stage for military actions that would follow in the coming years.
events.name: Sukarno's announcement on West Irian

events.enhanced_description: On January 3, 1961, U.S. President Dwight D. Eisenhower announced the severance of diplomatic and consular relations with Cuba, marking a significant turning point in U.S.-Cuba relations that would last for decades. This decision was influenced by the Cuban Revolution and the rise of Fidel Castro.
events.name: U.S. Severance of Relations with Cuba

events.enhanced_description: On January 5, 1961, Italian sculptor Alfredo Fioravanti entered the U.S. Consulate in Rome and confessed to being part of the team that forged the Etruscan terracotta warriors displayed at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. This revelation raised significant questions about art authenticity and provenance.
events.name: Confession of Forgery by Alfredo Fioravanti

events.enhanced_description: On January 7, 1961, following a four-day conference in Casablanca, five African leaders announced plans for a NATO-type organization to ensure mutual defense among African nations. This initiative aimed to strengthen regional security and cooperation amidst the backdrop of decolonization.
events.name: Casablanca Conference Announcement

events.enhanced_description: On January 8, 1961, a referendum in France supported President Charles de Gaulle's policies regarding Algerian independence. This vote was a critical moment in the decolonization process, reflecting the shifting attitudes towards colonial rule.
events.name: Referendum on Algerian Independence in France

events.enhanced_description: On January 9, 1961, British authorities announced the uncovering of a significant Soviet spy ring, known as the Portland spy ring, in London. This revelation highlighted the ongoing tensions of the Cold War and the pervasive nature of espionage during this period.
events.name: Uncovering of the Portland Spy Ring

events.enhanced_description: On January 17, 1961, President Dwight D. Eisenhower delivered his final State of the Union Address to Congress, during which he warned of the growing influence of a 'military-industrial complex.' This address underscored his concerns about the implications of military spending on American democracy.
events.name: Eisenhower's Final State of the Union Address

events.enhanced_description: On January 20, 1961, John F. Kennedy was sworn in as the 35th President of the United States, marking a new era in American politics. His inaugural address famously called for a new generation to take on the challenges of the time, emphasizing themes of freedom and responsibility.
events.name: John F. Kennedy Sworn in as President

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1961, the Congress of Venezuela adopted a new constitution, which would remain in force until 1999. This constitution aimed to address the political and social challenges facing the nation during a period of significant change.
events.name: Adoption of New Constitution in Venezuela

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1961, a B-52 Stratofortress carrying two nuclear bombs crashed near Goldsboro, North Carolina. This incident raised serious concerns about nuclear safety and the potential consequences of military accidents during the Cold War.
events.name: Goldsboro B-52 Crash

events.enhanced_description: On January 25, 1961, President John F. Kennedy held the first live presidential news conference, where he addressed the nation regarding the release of two surviving crewmen from a reconnaissance aircraft incident involving the Soviet Union. This marked a significant moment in presidential communication, showcasing the increasing role of television in politics.
events.name: First Live Presidential News Conference

events.enhanced_description: On January 27, 1961, the Soviet submarine S-80 sank in the Barents Sea, resulting in the tragic loss of all 68 crew members on board. The incident highlighted the dangers of Cold War military operations and the risks faced by submariners during this tense period.
events.name: Sinking of Soviet Submarine S-80

events.enhanced_description: On January 28, 1961, 'Supercar', the first family sci-fi television series filmed in Supermarionation, premiered on ATV in the UK. Created by Gerry Anderson, the show was notable for its innovative use of puppetry and special effects, paving the way for future productions in the genre.
events.name: Debut of Supercar

events.enhanced_description: On January 30, 1961, President John F. Kennedy delivered his first State of the Union Address to Congress, outlining his administration's priorities and vision for the nation. This address set the tone for his presidency and emphasized the importance of civil rights and economic growth.
events.name: John F. Kennedy's First State of the Union Address

events.enhanced_description: On January 31, 1961, Ham, a 37-pound male chimpanzee, was launched into space aboard Mercury-Redstone 2 as part of NASA's Project Mercury. This mission was a crucial step in testing the spacecraft's capabilities to carry human astronauts, marking a significant milestone in the space race.
events.name: Ham's Spaceflight

events.enhanced_description: On February 1, 1961, the United States conducted its first test of the Minuteman I intercontinental ballistic missile. This test represented a significant advancement in U.S. military technology during the Cold War, enhancing the country's nuclear deterrent capabilities.
events.name: First Minuteman I Missile Test

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1961, the Portuguese Colonial War began in Angola, marking the start of a protracted conflict between Portuguese colonial forces and various nationalist movements. This war would eventually lead to Angola's independence in 1975.
events.name: Beginning of the Portuguese Colonial War

events.enhanced_description: On February 5, 1961, President Joseph Kasa-Vubu appointed Joseph Iléo as the new Prime Minister of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. This appointment came during a tumultuous period in the country's history, following the assassination of Patrice Lumumba.
events.name: Joseph Iléo Named Prime Minister

events.enhanced_description: On February 9, 1961, The Beatles performed at The Cavern Club in Liverpool for the first time under their name after returning from Hamburg. This performance marked a significant moment in their early career, leading to their rise in popularity.
events.name: The Beatles at The Cavern Club

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1961, the USSR launched Venera 1 towards Venus, marking the first Soviet attempt to explore the planet. This mission was part of a broader effort during the space race to achieve significant milestones in planetary exploration.

image.caption: Soviet postage stamp depicting the launch of the Venus space probe, with a globe and Venera 1.
image.credit: Post of the Soviet Union. — http://skandinav.eu/page67.htm
image.date_qualification: A stamp issued after the launch, depicting the event; the saved image date is 1961-04-07, not the launch date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Launch of Venera 1

events.enhanced_description: On February 13, 1961, the Congolese government announced that villagers had killed Patrice Lumumba, further complicating the political situation in the country following his earlier assassination. This event underscored the instability and violence that characterized the Congo during this period.
events.name: Announcement of Lumumba's Death

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1961, Element 103, Lawrencium, was first synthesized at the University of California, Berkeley. This discovery contributed to the field of chemistry and the understanding of heavy elements.
events.name: Discovery of Lawrencium

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1961, President John F. Kennedy issued a warning to the Soviet Union, urging them to refrain from interfering with the United Nations' efforts to stabilize the situation in the Congo. This statement reflected the ongoing tensions of the Cold War and the complexities of international diplomacy.
events.name: Kennedy's Warning to the Soviet Union

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1961, a total solar eclipse was visible across the southern part of Europe, captivating observers and scientists alike. This astronomical event provided an opportunity for research and public engagement with the science of eclipses.
events.name: The total solar eclipse of February 15, 1961

events.enhanced_description: On February 26, 1961, Hassan II was pronounced King of Morocco following the death of his father, King Mohammed V. His reign would be marked by significant political changes and modernization efforts in Morocco.
events.name: Hassan II Becomes King of Morocco

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1961, President John F. Kennedy established the Peace Corps, a volunteer program aimed at promoting world peace and friendship. This initiative encouraged American citizens to serve in developing countries, fostering cultural exchange and development.
events.name: Establishment of the Peace Corps

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1961, Hassan II was crowned King of Morocco, succeeding his father, Mohammed V. His reign would be marked by significant political changes and modernization efforts in Morocco.
events.name: Crowning of Hassan II

events.enhanced_description: The Kungälv school shooting on March 4, 1961, was a tragic event where a gunman opened fire in a school, resulting in multiple casualties. This incident raised concerns about gun violence and school safety in Sweden and prompted discussions on mental health and societal issues.
events.name: Kungälv school shooting

events.enhanced_description: On March 8, 1961, aviator Max Conrad set a new world record by circumnavigating the Earth in a light plane in just 8 days, 18 hours, and 49 minutes. This remarkable feat showcased advancements in aviation and endurance flying.
events.name: Max Conrad's circumnavigation record

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1961, the Ken doll was introduced in the United States, becoming the first boyfriend of the iconic Barbie doll. This addition to the Barbie line marked a significant moment in toy history and popular culture.
events.name: Introduction of Ken doll

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1961, a dam burst in Kyiv, Ukraine, leading to the Kurenivka mudslide that resulted in the tragic loss of 145 lives. This disaster highlighted the risks associated with infrastructure failures in urban areas.
events.name: Kurenivka mudslide

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1961, South Africa announced its intention to withdraw from the Commonwealth of Nations as it transitioned to a republic. This decision was influenced by the country's growing isolation due to its apartheid policies.
events.name: South Africa withdraws from the Commonwealth

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1961, a ceasefire took effect in the Algerian War of Independence, marking a significant step towards the end of a brutal conflict that lasted from 1954 to 1962. This agreement paved the way for Algeria's eventual independence from France.
events.name: Ceasefire in the Algerian War of Independence

events.enhanced_description: On March 29, 1961, the Twenty-third Amendment to the United States Constitution was ratified, granting residents of Washington, D.C. the right to vote in presidential elections. This amendment was a significant step towards ensuring democratic representation for the nation's capital.
events.name: Ratification of the Twenty-third Amendment

events.enhanced_description: On March 30, 1961, the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs was signed in New York City, aiming to consolidate and regulate international drug control. This treaty represented a significant effort to combat drug abuse and trafficking globally.
events.name: Signing of the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1961, the New Guinea Council of Western Papua was installed, marking a significant step in the political development of the region. This council aimed to provide local governance and representation for the indigenous population.
events.name: New Guinea Council of Western Papua installed

events.enhanced_description: On April 8, 1961, the MV Dara, a passenger ship operated by the British India Steam Navigation Company, exploded and sank off the coast of Dubai, resulting in the tragic loss of 238 lives. The explosion was attributed to a fire that ignited a cargo of explosives on board.
events.name: MV Dara disaster

events.enhanced_description: On April 10, 1961, South African golfer Gary Player made history by becoming the first non-American to win the prestigious Masters Tournament at Augusta National Golf Club. His victory marked a significant moment in golf, showcasing the sport's growing international appeal.
events.name: Gary Player wins the Masters Tournament

events.enhanced_description: The trial of Nazi war criminal Adolf Eichmann began on April 11, 1961, in Jerusalem, Israel. Eichmann was charged with crimes against humanity for his role in orchestrating the logistics of the Holocaust, and the trial was a pivotal moment in the post-war reckoning with Nazi atrocities.
events.name: Trial of Adolf Eichmann

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1961, Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human to travel into space, orbiting the Earth aboard Vostok 1. This monumental achievement marked a significant milestone in the Space Race and human exploration of outer space.
events.name: Yuri Gagarin's spaceflight

events.enhanced_description: On April 13, 1961, a coup attempt against Portuguese Prime Minister António de Oliveira Salazar failed, highlighting the political tensions within Portugal during his authoritarian regime. The incident underscored the growing unrest and opposition to Salazar's government.
events.name: Failed coup against Salazar

events.enhanced_description: The U.S.-backed Bay of Pigs Invasion of Cuba commenced on April 17, 1961, aiming to overthrow Fidel Castro's government. The invasion ultimately failed, leading to significant political repercussions for the United States and solidifying Castro's power.

image.caption: Counter-attack by Cuban Revolutionary Armed Forces, supported by T-34 tanks, near Playa Girón during the Bay of Pigs Invasion.
image.date_qualification: Depicted date: 19 April 1961. The image_date field gives the original upload date, not the depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Bay of Pigs Invasion begins

events.enhanced_description: On April 18, 1961, Portugal dispatched its first military reinforcements to Angola in response to rising nationalist movements seeking independence. This action marked the beginning of a prolonged conflict in the region.
events.name: Portugal sends military to Angola

events.enhanced_description: On April 20, 1961, Fidel Castro publicly declared the defeat of the Bay of Pigs Invasion, solidifying his regime's legitimacy and strengthening anti-American sentiment in Cuba. This event was a significant victory for Castro and the Cuban Revolution.
events.name: Fidel Castro announces defeat of Bay of Pigs Invasion

events.enhanced_description: On April 22, 1961, four French generals attempted a coup in Algiers against President Charles de Gaulle, opposing his policies regarding Algerian independence. The coup ultimately failed, demonstrating the deep divisions within French society over the Algerian War.
events.name: Algiers putsch

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1961, Judy Garland performed a legendary comeback concert at Carnegie Hall in New York City, which is often regarded as one of the greatest live performances in music history. The concert revitalized her career and showcased her extraordinary talent.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Judy Garland's concert at Carnegie Hall

events.enhanced_description: On April 24, 1961, the Swedish warship Vasa, which sank on its maiden voyage in 1628, was successfully recovered from Stockholm Harbor. This event was a significant archaeological achievement and led to extensive restoration efforts, making the Vasa a prominent museum exhibit.
events.name: Recovery of the Vasa

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1961, Sierra Leone gained independence from the United Kingdom, marking a significant milestone in the decolonization movement in Africa. The transition to self-governance was celebrated as a moment of national pride for the Sierra Leonean people.

image.caption: Historical flag of Sierra Leone.
image.credit: Pbroks13 — https://www.crwflags.com/fotw/images/s/sl~1916.gif ; File:Government Ensign of the United Kingdom.svg
image.date_qualification: The image is a depiction of a historical flag, not a photograph of the independence event; the supplied image date is 2019-05-26.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Sierra Leone independence

events.enhanced_description: On May 15, 1961, J. Heinrich Matthaei conducted the Poly-U-Experiment, marking a pivotal moment in the understanding of the genetic code. This experiment demonstrated how RNA could be translated into proteins, laying the groundwork for modern genetics.
events.name: Poly-U-Experiment

events.enhanced_description: On May 16, 1961, Park Chung Hee led a military coup in South Korea, overthrowing the government of President Yun Bo-seon. This event marked the beginning of a military regime that would last for over a decade, significantly impacting South Korea's political landscape.
events.name: Military coup in South Korea

events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1961, Venera 1 became the first man-made object to fly by another planet, passing Venus. Unfortunately, the probe had lost contact with Earth a month earlier and did not transmit any data back.
events.name: Venera 1 flyby of Venus

events.enhanced_description: On May 21, 1961, Alabama Governor John Patterson declared martial law in response to escalating race riots in Montgomery. This decision was part of the broader civil rights movement, which sought to address racial segregation and discrimination.
events.name: Martial law declared in Alabama

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1961, New South Wales experienced a significant earthquake, causing damage and disruption in the region. This event highlighted the geological activity in Australia and raised awareness about earthquake preparedness.

image.caption: Relief location map of New South Wales, Australia.
image.credit: Tentotwo — DEM: CleanTOPO 2 Shaded relief, coastline, boundaries, rivers and lakes: Natural Earth
image.date_qualification: Map dated 2013-02-03; contextual map, not a contemporaneous image of the 1961 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: 1961 New South Wales earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1961, Freedom Riders were arrested in Jackson, Mississippi, for 'disturbing the peace' after disembarking from their bus. This event was part of a larger movement to challenge segregation in the South.
events.name: Freedom Riders arrested in Jackson

events.enhanced_description: On May 25, 1961, President John F. Kennedy addressed a special joint session of Congress, announcing his ambitious goal to land a man on the Moon before the end of the decade. This speech galvanized support for the Apollo program and the space race.
events.name: Kennedy's Moon speech

events.enhanced_description: On May 27, 1961, Tunku Abdul Rahman, the Prime Minister of Malaya, held a press conference in Singapore to announce his proposal for the formation of the Federation of Malaysia. This federation would include Malaya, Singapore, Sarawak, Brunei, and North Borneo.
events.name: Formation of the Federation of Malaysia

events.enhanced_description: On May 28, 1961, Peter Benenson's article 'The Forgotten Prisoners' was published in several major newspapers, which later led to the founding of Amnesty International. This marked a significant moment in the global human rights movement.
events.name: Publication of 'The Forgotten Prisoners'

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1961, Rafael Leónidas Trujillo, the long-time dictator of the Dominican Republic, was assassinated in an ambush. His death marked the end of a brutal regime that had lasted over three decades.
events.name: Assassination of Rafael Trujillo

events.enhanced_description: On May 31, 1961, in Paris, rebel generals Maurice Challe and André Zeller were sentenced to 15 years in prison for their roles in the Algerian War. This event underscored the tensions surrounding France's colonial policies.
events.name: Sentencing of rebel generals in France

events.enhanced_description: On June 1, 1961, Ethiopia experienced its most devastating earthquake of the 20th century, registering a magnitude of 6.7. The quake caused widespread destruction, leaving thousands homeless and highlighting the region's vulnerability to natural disasters.

locations.name: Majete
locations.region: Southern Nations, Nationalities, and Peoples' Region

events.name: Ethiopia earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On June 4, 1961, the Vienna summit took place where U.S. President John F. Kennedy met with Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev. The discussions focused on critical issues such as nuclear disarmament and the status of Germany during the Cold War.
events.name: Vienna summit

events.enhanced_description: On June 12, 1961, a patent was applied for the body electrode invented by Richard M. Berman and Bernard Schwartz. This invention contributed to advancements in medical technology and diagnostics.
events.name: Patent for body electrode

events.enhanced_description: On June 16, 1961, Soviet ballet dancer Rudolf Nureyev defected to the West at Paris–Le Bourget Airport while on tour with the Kirov Ballet. His defection was a significant cultural event during the Cold War, showcasing the tensions between East and West.
events.name: Rudolf Nureyev defects

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1961, a Paris-to-Strasbourg train derailed near Vitry-le-François, resulting in 24 fatalities and 109 injuries. This tragic incident raised concerns about railway safety in France.
events.name: Train derailment near Vitry-le-François

events.enhanced_description: On June 19, 1961, the British protectorate over Kuwait officially ended, and Kuwait became an independent emirate. This transition marked a significant step in the decolonization process in the Middle East.
events.name: End of British protectorate in Kuwait

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1961, Moise Tshombe was released from custody due to a lack of evidence connecting him to the murder of Patrice Lumumba. This event was significant in the political turmoil of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
events.name: Moise Tshombe released

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1961, the Antarctic Treaty came into effect, establishing Antarctica as a zone for peaceful scientific research and banning military activity on the continent. This treaty was a landmark agreement in international relations.
events.name: Antarctic Treaty comes into effect

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1961, Iraqi President Abd al-Karim Qasim announced his intention to annex newly independent Kuwait, a move that would later culminate in the Gulf War in 1990. This declaration heightened tensions in the region.
events.name: Iraq's intention to annex Kuwait

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1961, Kuwait requested British assistance against the Iraqi threat, leading to the deployment of British troops to the region. This military intervention was crucial in maintaining Kuwait's sovereignty during a period of instability.
events.name: British troops sent to Kuwait

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1961, the Soviet submarine K-19 experienced a severe reactor leak while operating in the North Atlantic. The incident posed a significant risk to the crew and highlighted the dangers associated with early nuclear submarines.
events.name: Soviet submarine K-19 suffers a reactor leak

events.enhanced_description: On July 5, 1961, Israel successfully launched its first rocket, Shavit 2, from Palmachim Airbase. This event marked a significant milestone in Israel's aerospace capabilities and its pursuit of technological advancement.
events.name: The first Israeli rocket, Shavit 2, is launched

events.enhanced_description: On July 8, 1961, a catastrophic mine explosion in Czechoslovakia resulted in the deaths of 108 individuals. This tragic event underscored the dangers associated with mining operations during this era.
events.name: A mine explosion in Czechoslovakia leaves 108 dead

events.enhanced_description: On July 12, 1961, a Czechoslovakian Ilyushin Il-18 aircraft crashed while attempting to land in Casablanca, Morocco, resulting in the tragic loss of all 72 passengers and crew on board. This incident raised concerns about aviation safety standards at the time.
events.name: A Czechoslovakian Ilyushin Il-18 crashes in Morocco

events.enhanced_description: On July 19, 1961, Trans World Airlines made history by becoming the first airline to show regularly scheduled movies during its flights, presenting 'By Love Possessed' to first-class passengers. This innovation transformed the in-flight experience for travelers.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Trans World Airlines shows first in-flight movie

events.enhanced_description: On July 21, 1961, astronaut Gus Grissom piloted the Mercury-Redstone 4 spacecraft, Liberty Bell 7, becoming the second American to travel into space. Following a successful sub-orbital flight, the spacecraft sank after a premature hatch opening during splashdown.
events.name: Gus Grissom's Mercury-Redstone 4 flight

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1961, U.S. President John F. Kennedy delivered a pivotal television address regarding the Berlin Crisis, asserting that the United States would not be driven out of Berlin. His speech emphasized the importance of civil defense and prompted a national discussion on fallout shelters.
events.name: John F. Kennedy's Berlin Crisis speech

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1961, the first tie in Major League Baseball All-Star Game history occurred at Fenway Park in Boston when the game was halted in the 9th inning due to rain. This unique outcome remained the only tie until 2002.

locations.name: Fenway Park, Boston, Massachusetts, United States

events.name: First Major League Baseball All-Star Game tie

events.enhanced_description: In August 1961, the United States initiated the Alliance for Progress, a program aimed at fostering economic cooperation and development in Latin America. This initiative was part of a broader strategy to counteract communism in the region.
events.name: The United States founds the Alliance for Progress

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1961, Six Flags Over Texas opened its doors to the public in Arlington, Texas, becoming the first theme park in the Six Flags chain. This park set the standard for future amusement parks with its innovative attractions and themed areas.

image.caption: The Silver Star Carousel and fountains at Six Flags Over Texas’s entry plaza.
image.date_qualification: A 2023 photograph of the park site and attractions, not a depiction of the 1961 opening.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Six Flags Over Texas theme park officially opens

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1961, Soviet cosmonaut Gherman Titov became the second human to orbit the Earth aboard Vostok 2, spending over a day in space. His mission demonstrated the Soviet Union's advancements in space exploration during the Cold War.

image.caption: Vostok 2 mission patch.
image.date_qualification: The mission took place on August 6, 1961; no depicted date is supplied for the patch. The listed 2008 timestamp is an upload/metadata date, not a depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Vostok 2: Gherman Titov orbits the Earth

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1961, Vostok 2 successfully landed back in the Soviet Union, concluding Gherman Titov's historic mission as the second human to orbit the Earth. This mission further solidified the USSR's position in the space race.

image.caption: Vostok 2 mission patch.
image.date_qualification: Mission insignia associated with Vostok 2; it is not a photograph of the spacecraft landing. No depicted image date is supplied.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Vostok 2 lands in the Soviet Union

events.enhanced_description: On August 10, 1961, the United Kingdom formally applied for membership in the European Economic Community (EEC), seeking to strengthen its economic ties with Europe. This application was a pivotal moment in the UK's post-war foreign policy.
events.name: The United Kingdom applies for EEC membership

events.enhanced_description: On August 11, 1961, an annular solar eclipse was visible from the Southern Ocean, captivating observers and astronomers alike. This astronomical event highlighted the beauty and rarity of solar eclipses.
events.name: An annular solar eclipse is visible from the Southern Ocean

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1961, construction of the Berlin Wall commenced, a pivotal event during the Berlin Crisis that physically and ideologically divided East and West Berlin. This barrier became a symbol of the Cold War and the struggle between communism and democracy.

image.caption: Exhibition about the Berlin Wall at Potsdamer Platz Arkaden.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2014-10-22; the event began 1961-08-13.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Construction of the Berlin Wall begins

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 1961, Jomo Kenyatta, a key figure in Kenya's struggle for independence, was released from prison. His release marked a significant step towards the eventual independence of Kenya from British colonial rule.
events.name: Jomo Kenyatta is released from prison

events.enhanced_description: On August 25, 1961, João Goulart assumed the presidency of Brazil, succeeding Jânio Quadros, who had resigned. Goulart's presidency would later be marked by political turmoil and his eventual ousting in a military coup in 1964.
events.name: João Goulart replaces Jânio Quadros as President of Brazil

events.enhanced_description: On August 29, 1961, a French military aircraft accidentally clipped a cable of the aerial tramway connecting Pointe Helbronner and the Aiguille du Midi in the French Alps. This tragic incident resulted in the fall of three tramway cars, claiming the lives of five individuals, while 63 other passengers were successfully rescued.

locations.historical_name: Pointe Helbronner and Aiguille du Midi
locations.name: Pointe Helbronner and Aiguille du Midi

events.name: French military aircraft tramway incident

events.enhanced_description: On August 30, 1961, the Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness was signed at the United Nations in New York City. This important treaty aimed to address the issues faced by stateless individuals and came into effect on December 13, 1975.

image.caption: Map showing parties to the Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness, signatories that have not ratified, and non-members.
image.credit: Ratherous — Own work . Data taken from [1] .
image.date_qualification: Map dated 2020-01-15; it is not a depiction of the 1961 signing event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness

events.enhanced_description: The Eritrean War of Independence commenced on September 1, 1961, marked by the Battle of Adal, where Hamid Idris Awate and his companions engaged Ethiopian police and military forces. This conflict would persist until 1991, ultimately leading to Eritrea's independence.
events.name: Eritrean War of Independence begins

events.enhanced_description: On September 7, 1961, the beloved animated series Tom and Jerry made a comeback with the release of 'Switchin' Kitten', marking the first new short since 1958. Under the direction of Gene Deitch, a total of 13 new shorts were produced through 1962.
events.name: Tom and Jerry return with Switchin' Kitten

events.enhanced_description: During the Italian Grand Prix on September 10, 1961, tragedy struck when German driver Wolfgang von Trips crashed his Ferrari into a spectator stand, resulting in the deaths of 14 spectators and himself. This incident raised significant concerns about safety in motorsport.
events.name: Italian Grand Prix tragedy

events.enhanced_description: On September 12, 1961, the African and Malagasy Union was established, aiming to promote unity and cooperation among African nations. This organization laid the groundwork for future regional cooperation in Africa.
events.name: African and Malagasy Union founded

events.enhanced_description: On September 14, 1961, Turkey's new military government sentenced 15 members of the previous government to death, reflecting the political turmoil following the military coup earlier that year. This marked a significant moment in Turkey's political history.

image.caption: Portrait of Hasan Polatkan.
image.credit: Uploader: Pivox, Hasan Polatkan — Demokrat Parti Türkiye Cumhuriyeti Tarihinin Başarısız Darbe Girişimi: Talat Aydemir Olayı başlığıyla alakalı olarak yayınlanan gazete haberinde Hasan Polatkan , 1940
image.date_qualification: The image description dates the portrait to 1940. The supplied 2017-03-03 image_date is not the depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Turkey's military government sentences former officials

events.enhanced_description: On September 17, 1961, military rulers in Turkey executed former Prime Minister Adnan Menderes, along with former Foreign Minister Fatin Rüştü Zorlu and former Finance Minister Hasan Polatkan. This event marked a dark chapter in Turkey's political history following the 1960 coup.
events.name: Execution of Turkish officials

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1961, Dag Hammarskjöld, the Secretary-General of the United Nations, tragically died in an air crash while en route to Katanga, Congo. His death raised significant concerns regarding the safety of UN officials and the political climate in Africa.
events.name: Dag Hammarskjöld dies in air crash

events.enhanced_description: On September 19, 1961, Barney and Betty Hill, an American couple, claimed to have witnessed a UFO while returning from Canada through New Hampshire. Their subsequent claims of alien abduction became one of the first widely publicized cases of such an experience, sparking interest in UFO phenomena.
events.name: Barney and Betty Hill UFO sighting

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1961, the Organisation de l'armée secrète (OAS) infiltrated French television programming to broadcast an anti-de Gaulle message. This act highlighted the tensions in France during the Algerian War and the opposition to Charles de Gaulle's policies.
events.name: OAS anti-de Gaulle message

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1961, the old Deutsche Opernhaus in the Charlottenburg neighborhood of Berlin was returned to its newly rebuilt house, now known as the Deutsche Oper Berlin. This marked a significant cultural revival in post-war Germany.
events.name: Deutsche Oper Berlin reopens

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1961, a military coup in Damascus, Syria, effectively ended the United Arab Republic, the political union between Egypt and Syria. This event marked a significant shift in the political landscape of the Middle East.
events.name: Syrian coup d'état

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1961, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) was formed to replace the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC). This organization aimed to promote policies that improve the economic and social well-being of people around the world.
events.name: OECD formation
